It sounds like all of the technology the researchers are talking about is going to be a self-healing version of carbon fiber... Then they add in this crap about

The healing agent, made of carbon-based chemicals, is successfully working and expected to be applied to at least part of the mobile phone industry within five years.

which says nothing about it actually being clear, or working on the phone screen. This sounds like great technology, but why did they have to use such a bullshit hypothetical application to sensationalize the article? The important thing to take away from this is that airplanes could have wings that heal microfractures in midair, and so could cars, bike frames, and anything else that uses carbon fiber. They never really say if phone screens are a practical use for this thing though.

I'm not an expert, but a big part of carbon fiber is the gel coat that encases it. If the gel coat (which is clear) is able to heal itself, that technology can start making its way into other territories that can put it to work.

I have worked some with carbon fiber, in the form of motorcycle bodywork, and in my experience the clear coat is purely cosmetic and in fact optional rather than being "a big part of carbon fiber". I have never put it on the pieces I've worked with because I was working on racebikes where cosmetic finishing was not important. The carbon fiber process I worked with was exactly the same as working with fiberglass: you have a flexible fiber cloth and an epoxy resin which soaks into the cloth (fills the minute gaps between fibers, to be more accurate) which hardens when cured and provides stiffness and form. So if the healing agent is made of carbon-based chemicals, I think hbr is correct in concluding that it will not be clear and will not be relevant to phone screens.

While this would make an impact on our business, since cell phone screen replacements are our bread and butter, it would take at least 1-2 years after the tech becomes commonplace for us to really feel it. Also, it seems like this would only repair superficial cracks in the glass. There is so much more to a phone screen than just a sheet of glass that would still need to be replaced. Break the top layer of glass, and you're good, phone repairs itself. Break the digitizer underneath, or the LCD/OLED under that? You're going to need it repaired. Those parts aren't as straightforward to repair as simply filling in a crack.

Firstly: just stick at it! Practice makes perfect. I'm sure you'll improve after a while :).

Secondly, try not to think at all about the controller. Keep your eyes on the screen. Think of the controller as an extension of your body. You should be thinking "I want to aim to the left." not "I need to move the stick to the left."
